description: Standard circuit symbols, series and parallel rules, and how to use test equipment.
content_html:
Why Symbols and Rules Matter

Before any circuit can be built or analysed, it must be drawn correctly. Examiners award marks for circuits using the correct standard symbols — a battery drawn as a single line scores no marks even if the rest of the circuit is perfect. Equally, getting the voltage and current rules wrong can cascade errors through every subsequent calculation. This lesson gives you the foundations everything else builds on.

Quantities, Units and Symbols

Three quantities appear in almost every electronics calculation. Confusing their units is the most commonly penalised error in exams.

Key Fact

Quantity — Symbol — Unit — Unit symbol:
Voltage — V — volt — V
Current — I — ampere — A
Resistance — R — ohm — Ω

Always include the unit symbol in your answer. Writing “5” when the answer is “5 V” will cost you a mark. Voltage is measured in volts (V), current in amperes (A) and resistance in ohms (Ω). These three are linked by Ohm’s law, covered in the next lesson.

Standard Circuit Symbols

Circuit diagrams use internationally agreed symbols. You are expected to know and draw the symbols for these components: cell, battery (multiple cells), resistor (rectangle), variable resistor (rectangle with an arrow), lamp, LED (arrow pointing away from the triangle), diode (triangle with a bar), capacitor (two parallel lines), switch, relay, fuse, voltmeter (circle with V), ammeter (circle with A), LDR (resistor with arrows pointing inward), thermistor (resistor with a T or slanted line), npn transistor, MOSFET, operational amplifier (triangle with + and − inputs), AND gate, OR gate, NOT gate, NAND gate and NOR gate.

Use only these standard symbols in exam circuit drawings. A rough sketch of a real component — or any invented symbol — scores zero. The specification appendix shows the exact forms required.

Series Circuits

In a series circuit, all components sit on a single loop. Two key rules apply:

  • Current is the same everywhere. If 20 mA flows through one resistor in a series chain, 20 mA flows through every other component in that chain.
  • Voltages add up. The sum of the voltages across each component equals the supply voltage: \(V_S = V_1 + V_2 + V_3\). This is a consequence of Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law.
Key Fact

Series circuit rules: current is the same at every point; voltages across each component add up to the supply voltage: \(V_S = V_1 + V_2 + \ldots\)

Parallel Circuits

In a parallel circuit, each branch connects directly between the same two points. Two rules apply:

  • Voltage is the same across every branch. A 9 V supply means 9 V appears across every parallel branch.
  • Currents add up at junctions. The total current from the supply equals the sum of the currents in all parallel branches: \(I_T = I_1 + I_2 + I_3\). This is Kirchhoff’s Current Law.

Series example: A 9 V supply drives two resistors in series. Voltmeter across R1 reads 4 V. What is the voltage across R2?

\(V_S = V_1 + V_2\) ⇒ \(9 = 4 + V_2\) ⇒ \(V_2 = 5 \text{ V}\)

Parallel example: Two branches carry 30 mA and 20 mA. What current does the supply deliver?

\(I_T = I_1 + I_2 = 30 + 20 = 50 \text{ mA}\)

Test Equipment

You need to know how to connect and use four instruments:

  • Voltmeter — always connected in parallel with the component being measured. Has very high input resistance so it draws negligible current.
  • Ammeter — always connected in series in the branch being measured. Has very low resistance so it introduces minimal voltage drop.
  • Logic probe — detects HIGH or LOW logic levels in digital circuits. It lights a different LED for logic 1 and logic 0, useful for testing gate outputs quickly.
  • Oscilloscope — displays a graph of voltage against time. The horizontal axis is time (controlled by the time-base setting, in ms/div or μs/div); the vertical axis is voltage (controlled by the Y-gain, in V/div or mV/div). Used to measure waveform amplitude, period and frequency.

A multimeter can measure voltage, current or resistance. Selecting the wrong mode — for example, connecting it in parallel on the current setting — can damage the instrument because it presents almost zero resistance across the supply.

A signal generator produces test waveforms. Three types appear in the specification:

Sine wave — a smoothly varying AC signal. The oscilloscope shows a regular S-curve. Amplitude is the peak height above zero, measured in volts from the centre line to the peak (NOT peak-to-peak).

Square wave — switches instantly between HIGH and LOW. Used to test digital circuits. Each half-period at HIGH and LOW should be equal for a 50% duty cycle.

Triangular wave — rises and falls linearly at a constant rate. Used for testing linearity of circuits.

Reading an oscilloscope: count the number of divisions for one complete cycle horizontally and multiply by the time-base value to get the period T. Frequency \(f = \frac{1}{T}\). For amplitude, count divisions from the centre to the peak and multiply by the Y-gain.
exam_tip_html: Oscilloscope reading questions are worth 3 marks and consistently lose students marks for unit confusion. Always write down the time-base value and the Y-gain value before calculating anything. Amplitude is measured from the centre line to the peak (NOT the full peak-to-peak distance). Period is the time for one complete cycle. If you calculate frequency, show \(f = 1/T\) explicitly — examiners award a mark for the correct method even if you make an arithmetic error. When asked to draw a circuit, use only standard symbols: a scruffy but correctly symbolised circuit beats a neat but non-standard one every time.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Voltage is in volts (V), current in amperes (A) and resistance in ohms (Ω). Always include units in every answer.
  • Series circuits: current is the same everywhere; voltages add to the supply. Parallel circuits: voltage is the same across every branch; currents add at junctions.
  • A voltmeter connects in parallel; an ammeter in series. On an oscilloscope, amplitude is centre-to-peak (not peak-to-peak), and period is the time for one complete cycle.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes how an ammeter is connected in a circuit?
A) In parallel with the component being measured
B) In series in the branch being measured
C) In parallel with the power supply
D) In series with the voltmeter
practice_questions.marks: B) In series in the branch being measured [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A student connects a 12 V supply to three resistors in series. The voltages across R1 and R2 are 3 V and 5 V respectively. Calculate the voltage across R3.
practice_questions.marks:
\(V_S = V_1 + V_2 + V_3\) [1 mark for correct equation or method]
\(V_3 = 12 - 3 - 5 = 4 \text{ V}\) [1 mark for correct answer with unit]

practice_questions.text: A parallel circuit has three branches carrying currents of 15 mA, 25 mA and 10 mA. Calculate the total current supplied by the battery.
practice_questions.marks:
\(I_T = I_1 + I_2 + I_3\) [1 mark for correct equation or method]
\(I_T = 15 + 25 + 10 = 50 \text{ mA}\) [1 mark for correct answer with unit]

practice_questions.text:
An oscilloscope displays a sine wave. The time-base is set to 2 ms/div and the Y-gain to 0.5 V/div. The wave occupies 4 divisions for one complete cycle and the peak reaches 3 divisions above the centre line.
(a) Calculate the period of the wave.
(b) Calculate the frequency of the wave.
(c) State the amplitude of the wave.
practice_questions.type: 3 marks — Read Off Graph or Oscilloscope
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Period = 4 div × 2 ms/div = 8 ms [1 mark]
(b) \(f = 1/T = 1/(8 \times 10^{-3}) = 125 \text{ Hz}\) [1 mark, accept 0.125 kHz]
(c) Amplitude = 3 div × 0.5 V/div = 1.5 V [1 mark — must be centre-to-peak, not peak-to-peak]

practice_questions.text: Explain why connecting a multimeter set to current-measurement mode directly across a power supply can damage the instrument.
practice_questions.marks: On the current setting, the multimeter has very low (near-zero) internal resistance [1 mark], so connecting it in parallel across the supply creates a near-short circuit, causing a very large current to flow through the instrument [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A student builds a series circuit with a 9 V supply, a 470 Ω resistor and an LED. The student then moves the LED into a parallel branch alongside the resistor (keeping the 470 Ω still in the circuit). Analyse how the voltage across the LED and the current through the LED change between the two configurations. Use Kirchhoff’s laws to support your answer.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Circuit Analysis and Evaluation
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise application of Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law to the series circuit (voltage shared between resistor and LED; LED voltage less than 9 V) and Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law to the parallel configuration (full 9 V appears across the LED branch). Recognition that 9 V is likely to destroy the LED (forward voltage typically 2 V for red LED) because the resistor is no longer in series to limit current. Quantitative reasoning: in series, V_LED = 9 V minus the voltage across the resistor; in parallel, V_LED = 9 V. Current in series is controlled by the resistor; in parallel the LED sees the full supply with no series resistor, so current is limited only by the LED’s own very low resistance, causing excessive current. Justified conclusion that the parallel configuration without a series resistor in the LED branch will damage the LED.
Secure: Correct direction of change for both voltage and current with Kirchhoff’s law referenced; LED damage predicted; explanation may lack precise quantitative detail.
Developing: Voltage or current change identified correctly for at least one configuration; limited use of Kirchhoff’s law; partial conclusion.
Emerging: Simple statement that the LED gets more/less voltage with no law-based reasoning.

knowledge_checks.q: In a series circuit with a 12 V supply and two resistors, the voltage across R1 is 7 V. What is the voltage across R2?
Which instrument is always connected in parallel with a component to measure the voltage across it?
In a parallel circuit, the voltage across each branch is _____ the supply voltage.
On an oscilloscope, the amplitude of a wave is measured from the _____ line to the peak.
Match each quantity to its correct SI unit:

flashcard_questions.q: What is the SI unit of electrical current?
What is the SI unit of electrical resistance?
In a series circuit, how does current compare at different points in the loop?
flashcard_questions.a: Current is the same at every point in the loop.

flashcard_questions.q: State the voltage rule for a series circuit (Kirchhoff's Voltage Law).
flashcard_questions.a: The sum of voltages across each component equals the supply voltage.

flashcard_questions.q: In a parallel circuit, how does voltage compare across each branch?
flashcard_questions.a: Voltage is the same across every parallel branch.

flashcard_questions.q: State the current rule at a junction in a parallel circuit (Kirchhoff's Current Law).
flashcard_questions.a: Total current from the supply equals the sum of branch currents.

flashcard_questions.q: How is a voltmeter connected in a circuit?
flashcard_questions.a: In parallel with the component being measured.

flashcard_questions.q: How is an ammeter connected in a circuit?
flashcard_questions.a: In series within the branch being measured.

flashcard_questions.q: On an oscilloscope, what does the time-base control?
flashcard_questions.a: The time represented by each horizontal division (e.g. ms/div).

flashcard_questions.q: On an oscilloscope, amplitude is measured from the centre line to the ___.
A signal generator produces a waveform that switches instantly between HIGH and LOW. What type of wave is this?
What does a logic probe detect in a digital circuit?
flashcard_questions.a: Whether a point is at logic HIGH or logic LOW.

glossary_terms.definition: A source of electrical energy, represented in a circuit diagram as a pair of parallel lines of unequal length (long line = positive terminal).
A circuit in which components are connected end-to-end so that the same current flows through every component.
A circuit in which components are connected across the same two nodes so that each component has the same voltage across it.
A multi-function test instrument that can measure voltage, current or resistance depending on the mode selected.
